Sixteen Years of 311: How Resolution Odds Changed Across Administrations

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Recorded resolution-time probabilities for NYC 311 service requests, 2010–2026, compared across mayoral administrations — citywide, by complaint type, and within individual census tracts.

Published

September 19, 2026

NoteHow to read this document

Plain-language takeaways open each section; the code that produced every number and figure is folded beneath it (click “Code”). To reproduce: run the pipeline in pipeline/ (fetch_311.py, fetch_311_history.py, prepare.py, prepare_hist.py), then render this file with quarto render docs/historical_analysis.qmd.

Summary

This analysis asks how the recorded probability that a 311 request gets resolved — within 3 hours, within a day, within a week — has moved since 2010, and whether different mayoral administrations are associated with different odds in the same census tract. Three design choices matter throughout:

  1. Within-type comparisons. What New Yorkers report changed enormously (the 311 app made noise complaints explode), and complaint types resolve at wildly different speeds. Comparing administrations on the all-complaints average mostly measures this composition shift, so every comparison here is within a complaint type.
  2. Recorded, not necessarily real. A “resolution” is the city closing the ticket. Closure practices (batch purges, auto-close policies) changed across eras; we flag and quantify these artifacts rather than pretend they don’t exist.
  3. COVID is its own era. March 2020 – December 2021 is a structural break and is never averaged into an administration’s record.
Setup: load 16 years of cleaned requests, define eras 
import glob, json, os, sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ROOT = ".." if os.path.basename(os.getcwd()) == "docs" else "."
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(ROOT, "pipeline"))
import model as M

ERAS = [
    ("bloomberg", "Bloomberg (final term)", "2010-01-01", "2014-01-01"),
    ("deblasio",  "de Blasio (pre-COVID)",  "2014-01-01", "2020-03-01"),
    ("covid",     "COVID emergency",        "2020-03-01", "2022-01-01"),
    ("adams",     "Adams",                  "2022-01-01", "2026-01-01"),
    ("current",   "Mamdani (2026)",         "2026-01-01", "2027-01-01"),
]
ERA_LABEL = {k: lb for k, lb, *_ in ERAS}

# conservative 1:1 taxonomy renames across the study period
RENAMES = {"HEATING": "HEAT/HOT WATER", "PAINT - PLASTER": "PAINT/PLASTER",
           "NONCONST": "UNSANITARY CONDITION", "Sewer Maintenance": "Sewer"}

parts = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "prepared_hist", "year=*.parquet")))
df = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(p) for p in parts]
               + [pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "prepared.parquet"))
                  .query("created_date >= '2025-01-01'")],   # prepared_hist already covers <=2024
               ignore_index=True)
df["created_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["created_date"])
for c in ["geoid", "nta", "boro", "complaint_type"]:
    df[c] = df[c].astype(str)
df.loc[df["geoid"].isin(["nan", "None", "<NA>"]), "geoid"] = np.nan
df["complaint_type"] = df["complaint_type"].replace(RENAMES)
df["era"] = pd.cut(df["created_date"],
                   bins=[pd.Timestamp(s) for _, _, s, _ in ERAS] + [pd.Timestamp(ERAS[-1][3])],
                   labels=[k for k, *_ in ERAS], right=False)
df = df[df["era"].notna()]
df["year"] = df["created_date"].dt.year
N_TOTAL = len(df)
SPAN = (df["created_date"].min().date(), df["created_date"].max().date())
era_keys = [k for k, *_ in ERAS if (df["era"] == k).any()]   # eras with data present

# dark theme to match the map app
C = {"bg": "#0B0E14", "text": "#F2F4F8", "sub": "#9AA3B5", "line": "#2A3244",
     "accent": "#FFB84D"}
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": C["bg"], "axes.facecolor": C["bg"], "savefig.facecolor": C["bg"],
    "axes.edgecolor": C["line"], "axes.labelcolor": C["sub"], "text.color": C["text"],
    "xtick.color": C["sub"], "ytick.color": C["sub"], "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.color": C["line"], "grid.linewidth": 0.5, "font.size": 11})

The analysis covers 40,670,321 cleaned, matured service requests created between 2010-01-01 and 2026-08-18, all passed through the identical hygiene rules as the live map (de-duplication, double-submission collapse, negative/zero-duration removal, batch-closure flagging, point-in-polygon assignment to 2020 census tracts — see docs/METHODS.md).

The data changed as much as the city did

Before comparing administrations, look at what the instrument itself was doing. Request volume roughly doubled; the complaint mix transformed; geocoding quality improved; and the share of requests never administratively closed varies by era. Every one of these can masquerade as a “service change.”

Era context table: volume, composition, artifact rates 
rows = []
for key, label, s, e in ERAS:
    sub = df[df["era"] == key]
    if len(sub) == 0:

    yrs = max((pd.Timestamp(e) - pd.Timestamp(s)).days / 365.25, 5 / 12)
    top3 = sub["complaint_type"].value_counts(normalize=True).head(3)
    rows.append({

        "requests/yr (M)": round(len(sub) / yrs / 1e6, 2),
        "share never closed": f'{(sub["bin"].eq(M.K - 1) & 1).mean():.1%}',

        "top complaint (share)": f"{top3.index[0].title()} ({top3.iloc[0]:.0%})",

WarningWhat this table means for interpretation

The comparisons below are of recorded closures under each era’s record-keeping practices. Where an era’s batch-closure or never-closed rates stand out, treat its differences as partly administrative. Tract geocoding also improves over time; rows without coordinates still inform borough and citywide estimates but not tract-level ones.

Select complaint types comparable across all five eras 
MIN_PER_ERA = 15_000
vol = df.groupby(["complaint_type", "era"], observed=True).size().unstack("era", fill_value=0)
stable = vol[(vol >= MIN_PER_ERA).all(axis=1)].sort_values("adams", ascending=False)
TYPES = stable.index.tolist()

Cross-era comparisons use the 27 complaint types that appear with meaningful volume (≥15,000 requests) in every era, after normalizing known renames (e.g., pre-2014 “HEATING” is today’s “Heat/Hot Water”): Illegal Parking, Noise - Residential, Heat/Hot Water, Blocked Driveway, Noise - Street/Sidewalk, Unsanitary Condition, Street Condition, Noise - Commercial, Plumbing, Water System, Noise, Paint/Plaster, Noise - Vehicle, Derelict Vehicles, Traffic Signal Condition, General Construction/Plumbing, Damaged Tree, Electric, Sewer, Street Light Condition, Sidewalk Condition, Maintenance Or Facility, Non-Emergency Police Matter, Appliance, Overgrown Tree/Branches, Elevator, Building/Use.

Within the same tract: administration deltas

The citywide picture can hide local reversals. Here we fit the same hierarchical Bayesian model that powers the live map (tract → neighborhood → borough → city, per complaint type; concentrations by marginal-likelihood MLE) separately to each era’s data, then difference the posterior same-day probabilities tract by tract. Only tracts with at least 30 requests of that type in both eras are compared, so the deltas reflect local evidence rather than shared priors.

Fit the hierarchical model per era; compute tract-level deltas 
geo = M.GeoIndex(json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "geo_lookup.json"))))
MIN_TRACT_N = 30
tix = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(TYPES + ["Other"])}

fits, counts = {}, {}
for key in era_keys:
    sub = df[df["era"] == key].copy()
    sub["ctype"] = M.collapse_types(sub["complaint_type"], TYPES)
    fits[key] = M.fit(sub, geo, TYPES + ["Other"], M.Config("era", half_life_days=None),
                      sub["created_date"].max())
    s2 = sub[sub["geoid"].notna()]
    counts[key] = s2.groupby([s2["geoid"], s2["ctype"]], observed=True).size()

def p24_and_var(fm):
    a = fm.a_tract; A = a.sum(-1); Ac = a[..., :2].sum(-1)
    m = Ac / A
    return m, m * (1 - m) / (A + 1)

def tract_deltas(a_key, b_key):
    ma, va = p24_and_var(fits[a_key]); mb, vb = p24_and_var(fits[b_key])
    out = {}
    for t in TYPES:
        ti = tix[t]; recs = []
        for g, gi in geo.tract_ix.items():
            if counts[a_key].get((g, t), 0) < MIN_TRACT_N: continue
            if counts[b_key].get((g, t), 0) < MIN_TRACT_N: continue
            d = ma[gi, ti] - mb[gi, ti]
            se = np.sqrt(va[gi, ti] + vb[gi, ti])
            recs.append((g, d, se))
        if len(recs) >= 25:
            dd = np.array([r[1] for r in recs])
            out[t] = {"recs": recs, "n": len(recs),
                      "med": np.median(dd),
                      "q10": np.percentile(dd, 10), "q90": np.percentile(dd, 90),
                      "up": np.mean([d - 1.645 * s > 0 for _, d, s in recs]),
                      "dn": np.mean([d + 1.645 * s < 0 for _, d, s in recs])}
    return out

D_ad = tract_deltas("adams", "deblasio")
D_ca = tract_deltas("current", "adams")

def delta_table(D):
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "tracts compared": {t.title(): v["n"] for t, v in D.items()},
        "median Δ (pts)": {t.title(): round(100 * v["med"], 1) for t, v in D.items()},
        "10th–90th pct": {t.title(): f'{100*v["q10"]:+.0f} … {100*v["q90"]:+.0f}'
                          for t, v in D.items()},
        "share sig. faster": {t.title(): f'{v["up"]:.0%}' for t, v in D.items()},
        "share sig. slower": {t.title(): f'{v["dn"]:.0%}' for t, v in D.items()},
    }).sort_values("median Δ (pts)", ascending=False)
Delta table: Adams vs de Blasio

Interpretation

(This section is written against the rendered numbers above; the inline values update automatically on re-render.)

Values referenced in the prose

                         else raw_all.loc[k])
noise_types = [t for t in TYPES if "Noise" in t]
noise_share = {k: df[df["era"] == k]["complaint_type"].isin(noise_types).mean()
               for k in era_keys}
raw_gain = raw_all.loc["adams"] - raw_all.loc["bloomberg"]
adj_gain = adj_all.loc["adams"] - adj_all.loc["bloomberg"]
covid_noise = noise_share.get("covid", float("nan"))

Findings that survive the composition and artifact controls:

  1. Most of the all-complaints “improvement” is composition. Raw same-day resolution rose from 37% (Bloomberg) to 58% (Adams) — but holding the complaint mix fixed, the rise is only 48% → 53%. Roughly 78% of the apparent improvement is the mix shifting toward fast-resolving categories (noise complaints grew from 13% of Bloomberg-era volume to 20% under Adams). Any claim that “311 got faster under mayor X” that doesn’t condition on complaint type is mostly measuring New Yorkers’ reporting habits.
  2. The clearest operational pattern is agency-shaped, not administration-shaped. Housing types (all handled by HPD) improved monotonically across every era: same-day resolution of Heat/Hot Water went 11% → 15% → 27% from Bloomberg to de Blasio to Adams, with Plumbing, Electric, and Paint/Plaster showing the same staircase from near-zero. Meanwhile infrastructure types slipped across the same span — Water System 66% → 62%, Traffic Signals 86% → 82% — and police-handled types (parking, noise) have been saturated near 99% for sixteen years. Secular agency trajectories dominate administration boundaries.
  3. Within types, administrations were not uniform across neighborhoods — see Table 1: the 10th–90th percentile spread of tract-level changes is wide even where the median change is small, and the tract map shows spatial clustering rather than uniform shifts.
  4. COVID was a composition shock more than a slowdown. The raw all-complaints series rose during 2020–21, because lockdown-era noise complaints surged to 25% of all volume; per-type effects ran in both directions (heat improved, derelict-vehicle and traffic-signal work slowed). This is exactly why the COVID window is quarantined and why the mix-adjusted row is the one to read.
  5. The Mamdani administration’s record is provisional (Table 2). Zohran Mamdani took office in January 2026, succeeding Eric Adams, so this era covers only the months of 2026 that have matured, is missing the autumn and early-winter months that every other era includes, and is best treated as a baseline for future updates rather than a verdict.

Why the live map still trains on recent data only

The dashboard deliberately ignores this history when estimating current odds. Its evaluation selected a 90-day exponential decay: under that weighting a two-year-old request carries weight 0.0036 — effectively zero — and the prior comparison showed shorter memory beats longer memory for near-term prediction (docs/evaluation_results.md). History answers “what changed”; the last two years answer “what should I expect if I call today.” Those are different questions, and this document exists so the map doesn’t have to answer both.

Caveats, stated plainly

  • Recorded ≠ experienced. Closure timestamps are administrative events. Era differences partly reflect record-keeping practice; batch-closure and never-closed rates are quantified in the era context table.
  • Bloomberg = final term only. The public dataset begins 2010; nothing here speaks to 2002–2009.
  • Geocoding improves over time (86% of 2010 requests are tract-mappable vs ~98% today), so early-era tract comparisons rest on a slightly thinner, possibly non-random subset of requests.
  • Taxonomy drift is handled conservatively: only unambiguous renames are merged, and analysis is restricted to types present in every era. Types born after 2014 (e.g., outdoor dining complaints) are simply out of scope for the long arc.
  • Administrations are periods, not causes. Nothing here identifies why a probability moved — budgets, laws, weather, and reporting behavior all changed concurrently. This is a descriptive account of associations within fixed geography.

Technical addendum: modeling decisions, sensitivity, and robustness

This appendix records the decisions behind the machinery this analysis reuses, and the checks run along the way. Numbers quoted from prior evaluations are the documented outputs of the pipeline’s own harnesses (docs/evaluation_results.md, docs/statistical_review.md); everything specific to this document is computed in the chunks above.

Model class

The estimator throughout is a hierarchical Dirichlet–Multinomial over the nine ordered duration bins, with partial pooling tract → NTA → borough → citywide, fit as a top-down conjugate cascade (each node’s Dirichlet prior is κ pseudo-counts shaped like its parent’s posterior mean). Alternatives considered and rejected: continuous-time survival models (non-conjugate inference at 40M rows for a deliverable that is the binned distribution anyway); continuation-ratio Beta–Binomial stacks (equally conjugate but no actual adjacent-bin smoothing without breaking conjugacy — bin order is instead respected at evaluation time via the ranked probability score); and full hierarchical Bayes with sampled concentrations (too slow for a weekly refresh of every cell). The plug-in shortcut was then checked against a fully Bayesian Stan fit for one borough and three complaint types: tract means differ by 0.7–1.1 points on average (docs/stan_validation.md). Pooling runs within complaint type across geography, not across types within a tract, because resolution speed is owned by the responsible agency, not the neighborhood.

Configuration contest (live map)

Nine configurations were compared on a temporal holdout (train 2024-08 → 2025-08, test the following 12 months; all hyperparameters fit on train only), scored by mean RPS (primary), log-loss, calibration error, and interval calibration, with paired block-bootstrap SEs over tract×type cells (docs/evaluation_results.md):

configuration RPS vs. best
No pooling (uniform / Jeffreys) 0.10685 / 0.10548 +0.00395 / +0.00258
Hierarchy, fixed κ=15 0.10365 +0.00075
Hierarchy, EB κ (per type / per type-level) 0.10316 / 0.10318 +0.00026 / +0.00028
+ 90-day decay (shipped) 0.10302 +0.00012
+ 180-day / 365-day decay 0.10290 / 0.10297 best / +0.00007

The no-pooling baselines’ failure mode is exact and diagnostic: on tract×type cells unseen in training they predict the bare prior — uniform over nine bins, log-loss log(9) = 2.197 — while the hierarchy falls back to the neighborhood estimate (1.73–1.88).

This single split trains once and predicts up to a year ahead, which favors long memory and is not how the map is used; the weekly-refit setting is tested by a rolling-origin evaluation that refits at each month start and scores only that month (docs/rolling_evaluation.md). There, half-lives of 45 to 180 days are statistically tied with the shipped 90 days (differences of 0.00000 to +0.00004 RPS), 365 days is worse by 0.00014 ± 0.00005, and no decay by 0.00040 ± 0.00008, so 90 days stays.

Defects found by audit, all fixed

Adversarial computational audits (independent re-implementation of the cascade; verification of every exported cell against the raw files) found:

  1. Concentration estimation under-converged. Minka’s fixed-point iteration stalled far short of the marginal-likelihood optimum on these flat surfaces (tract-level Heat/Hot Water: κ ≈ 230 vs true optimum ≈ 800, a 78-nat likelihood gap; Illegal Parking: 87 vs ≈ 400, 288 nats). The estimator now maximizes the exact Dirichlet–Multinomial marginal likelihood by bounded scalar optimization. Predictions moved negligibly (the flat surface is why the defect was silent), but pooling strengths are now genuine MLEs — including the era fits above.
  2. Raw posterior intervals badly under-covered. In the original audit, coverage of nominal 90% intervals on dense cells was 0.25–0.51 — including on an even/odd day-of-year split where drift is impossible by construction, refuting an initial “temporal drift” explanation. The live map’s intervals now add a per-type, per-threshold regime variance estimated from rolling 60-day temporal holdouts; on the current data, coverage is 0.908 in dense cells and about 0.90 in sparse ones (squared standardized residual 1.14). A multiplicative (design-effect) correction was tested and rejected — it absurdly inflates sparse-cell intervals. Why the even/odd-day shortfall occurred (correlated outcomes within cells is the working hypothesis) has not been tested directly.
  3. Requests without a tract were counted in one tract. Under pandas 2, converting the tract column with astype(str) turned missing values into the text “nan”, so about 1.6% of requests were counted in Rikers Island (tract 36005000100); pandas 3 keeps them missing, so the result depended on the installed version. Fixed, verified across versions, and guarded by export checks (docs/statistical_review.md §7). The era fits in this report were not affected: they load the data with their own null handling.
  4. Interval theory ignored the uncertainty of the borrowed neighborhood mean. A simulation with known truth showed 43–81% coverage for nominal 90% intervals even when the data follow the model exactly; the interval variance now includes that term (docs/simulation_check.md). On real data the regime variance dominates, so users see almost no change.

Sensitivity and robustness checks run

  • Decay half-life: rolling-origin comparison over 11 monthly refits (see above); 45–180 days are tied, 365 days and no decay are worse.
  • Seasonal blending: a same-season-last-year kernel (conjugate, weight β·2^(−|age−1yr|/bw)) was re-tested with two years of history under the same rolling protocol. The best variant improves RPS by 0.00013 ± 0.00004 and log-loss by 0.00176 ± 0.00038 but wins in only 5 of the 11 months, so it is not adopted (pipeline/eval_rolling.py).
  • Pooling strength per threshold: fitting a separate strength for each cumulative threshold improves held-out log-loss slightly at all eight thresholds, but is mixed by type and marginal for the all-complaints view; not adopted (docs/cutwise_evaluation.md). This bears on this report: the tract-level era comparisons use the nine-bin pooling, so for types where that over-pools the 24-hour rate, tract-level changes between eras are understated (conservative), not overstated.
  • Censoring: the 31-day maturity cutoff is keyed to the top bin boundary, making the “still open ⇒ month+” assignment deductively exact rather than imputed; verified against pull dates. Composition of the month+ bin was audited on the original window: 8.8% of matured requests land there, 28.5% of those never close; for Heat/Hot Water >99% of month+ cases are administrative non-closures — reported as-is with a high-open-share flag.
  • Cleaning funnel (current live window): 7.52M → 7.08M rows; about 286k double-submissions collapsed, 131k exact-zero durations dropped, 114k batch closures flagged and kept (dropping them would optimistically bias slow agencies). A full evaluation re-run excluding batch-flagged records remains open; for this document their per-era rates are disclosed in the era context table instead.
  • Independent audit (pipeline/audit.py): raw rows reconcile with the funnel; every tract × type count matches an independent tally; binning is correct at the bin boundaries; a separate re-implementation of the cascade reproduces all 51,150 cells; and one month recomputed from the raw files agrees with the pipeline to 0.1 point.
  • RPS implementation verified against hand computation; bootstrap resamples cells, not requests (within-cell correlation would otherwise understate SEs).

Choices specific to this historical analysis

  • Era fits use no decay: the estimand is each era’s average recorded behavior, not a nowcast. Concentrations are re-estimated per era, so pooling strength adapts to each era’s data density.
  • Stable-type restriction (≥15k requests in every era) plus conservative 1:1 rename normalization; types that split or merged across the 2014 taxonomy overhaul are excluded rather than guessed at.
  • Tract deltas require n ≥ 30 in both eras so differences reflect local evidence rather than two shared priors agreeing with each other; interval on the delta is the normal combination of the two independent Beta variances. This intentionally reports sampling uncertainty for a fixed-era estimand — the regime-variance component the live map adds is a forecasting correction and would be wrong here.
  • Composition adjustment fixes the complaint mix at the pooled all-era distribution; the raw-vs-adjusted gap isolates how much of each era’s apparent speed is reporting mix.
  • COVID quarantine (2020-03 – 2021-12) keeps an extraordinary operating regime out of both adjacent administrations’ records.
  • Known residual risks: geocoding coverage drift (86% → 98% tract-mappable); recorded-vs-experienced resolution; single-observation seasonality in the partial-year Mamdani era (2026), which lacks autumn and early winter.

Reproduction

python3 pipeline/fetch_311.py            # rolling two-year window
python3 pipeline/fetch_311_history.py    # 2010-2024 archive (~38M rows)
python3 pipeline/prepare.py && python3 pipeline/prepare_hist.py --all
quarto render docs/historical_analysis.qmd

Full detail: docs/model_spec.md (specification), docs/evaluation_results.md and docs/rolling_evaluation.md (evaluation), docs/statistical_review.md (audits), docs/METHODS.md (public methods).

Data: NYC Open Data — 311 Service Requests (2010–2019 archive 76ig-c548; 2020–present erm2-nwe9). Cleaning and model code: pipeline/ in this repository. Not affiliated with the City of New York.

## Summary

This analysis asks how the *recorded* probability that a 311 request gets resolved —
within 3 hours, within a day, within a week — has moved since 2010, and whether
different mayoral administrations are associated with different odds **in the same
census tract**. Three design choices matter throughout:

1. **Within-type comparisons.** What New Yorkers report changed enormously (the 311
   app made noise complaints explode), and complaint types resolve at wildly different
   speeds. Comparing administrations on the all-complaints average mostly measures
   this composition shift, so every comparison here is within a complaint type.
2. **Recorded, not necessarily real.** A "resolution" is the city closing the ticket.
   Closure practices (batch purges, auto-close policies) changed across eras; we flag
   and quantify these artifacts rather than pretend they don't exist.
3. **COVID is its own era.** March 2020 – December 2021 is a structural break and is
   never averaged into an administration's record.

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| code-summary: "Setup: load 16 years of cleaned requests, define eras"
import glob, json, os, sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ROOT = ".." if os.path.basename(os.getcwd()) == "docs" else "."
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(ROOT, "pipeline"))
import model as M

ERAS = [
    ("bloomberg", "Bloomberg (final term)", "2010-01-01", "2014-01-01"),
    ("deblasio",  "de Blasio (pre-COVID)",  "2014-01-01", "2020-03-01"),
    ("covid",     "COVID emergency",        "2020-03-01", "2022-01-01"),
    ("adams",     "Adams",                  "2022-01-01", "2026-01-01"),
    ("current",   "Mamdani (2026)",         "2026-01-01", "2027-01-01"),
]
ERA_LABEL = {k: lb for k, lb, *_ in ERAS}

# conservative 1:1 taxonomy renames across the study period
RENAMES = {"HEATING": "HEAT/HOT WATER", "PAINT - PLASTER": "PAINT/PLASTER",
           "NONCONST": "UNSANITARY CONDITION", "Sewer Maintenance": "Sewer"}

parts = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "prepared_hist", "year=*.parquet")))
df = pd.concat([pd.read_parquet(p) for p in parts]
               + [pd.read_parquet(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "prepared.parquet"))
                  .query("created_date >= '2025-01-01'")],   # prepared_hist already covers <=2024
               ignore_index=True)
df["created_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["created_date"])
for c in ["geoid", "nta", "boro", "complaint_type"]:
    df[c] = df[c].astype(str)
df.loc[df["geoid"].isin(["nan", "None", "<NA>"]), "geoid"] = np.nan
df["complaint_type"] = df["complaint_type"].replace(RENAMES)
df["era"] = pd.cut(df["created_date"],
                   bins=[pd.Timestamp(s) for _, _, s, _ in ERAS] + [pd.Timestamp(ERAS[-1][3])],
                   labels=[k for k, *_ in ERAS], right=False)
df = df[df["era"].notna()]
df["year"] = df["created_date"].dt.year
N_TOTAL = len(df)
SPAN = (df["created_date"].min().date(), df["created_date"].max().date())
era_keys = [k for k, *_ in ERAS if (df["era"] == k).any()]   # eras with data present

# dark theme to match the map app
C = {"bg": "#0B0E14", "text": "#F2F4F8", "sub": "#9AA3B5", "line": "#2A3244",
     "accent": "#FFB84D"}
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": C["bg"], "axes.facecolor": C["bg"], "savefig.facecolor": C["bg"],
    "axes.edgecolor": C["line"], "axes.labelcolor": C["sub"], "text.color": C["text"],
    "xtick.color": C["sub"], "ytick.color": C["sub"], "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.color": C["line"], "grid.linewidth": 0.5, "font.size": 11})
```

The analysis covers **`{python} f"{N_TOTAL:,}"`** cleaned, matured service requests
created between `{python} str(SPAN[0])` and `{python} str(SPAN[1])`, all passed
through the identical hygiene rules as the live map (de-duplication, double-submission
collapse, negative/zero-duration removal, batch-closure flagging, point-in-polygon
assignment to 2020 census tracts — see `docs/METHODS.md`).

## The data changed as much as the city did

Before comparing administrations, look at what the instrument itself was doing.
Request volume roughly doubled; the complaint mix transformed; geocoding quality
improved; and the share of requests never administratively closed varies by era.
Every one of these can masquerade as a "service change."

```{python}
#| label: artifacts
#| code-summary: "Era context table: volume, composition, artifact rates"
rows = []
for key, label, s, e in ERAS:
    sub = df[df["era"] == key]
    if len(sub) == 0:
        continue
    yrs = max((pd.Timestamp(e) - pd.Timestamp(s)).days / 365.25, 5 / 12)
    top3 = sub["complaint_type"].value_counts(normalize=True).head(3)
    rows.append({
        "era": label,
        "requests/yr (M)": round(len(sub) / yrs / 1e6, 2),
        "share never closed": f'{(sub["bin"].eq(M.K - 1) & 1).mean():.1%}',
        "batch-closure flagged": f'{sub["batch_closed"].mean():.1%}',
        "tract-geocoded": f'{sub["geoid"].notna().mean():.1%}',
        "top complaint (share)": f"{top3.index[0].title()} ({top3.iloc[0]:.0%})",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("era")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="What this table means for interpretation"}
The comparisons below are of **recorded closures under each era's record-keeping
practices**. Where an era's batch-closure or never-closed rates stand out, treat its
differences as partly administrative. Tract geocoding also improves over time; rows
without coordinates still inform borough and citywide estimates but not tract-level
ones.
:::

```{python}
#| label: stable-types
#| code-summary: "Select complaint types comparable across all five eras"
MIN_PER_ERA = 15_000
vol = df.groupby(["complaint_type", "era"], observed=True).size().unstack("era", fill_value=0)
stable = vol[(vol >= MIN_PER_ERA).all(axis=1)].sort_values("adams", ascending=False)
TYPES = stable.index.tolist()
```

Cross-era comparisons use the **`{python} len(TYPES)`** complaint types that appear
with meaningful volume (≥15,000 requests) in *every* era, after normalizing known
renames (e.g., pre-2014 "HEATING" is today's "Heat/Hot Water"):
`{python} ", ".join(t.title() for t in TYPES)`.

```{python}
#| label: mix-adjust
#| code-summary: "Composition-adjusted citywide same-day rate"
ctype_all = df["complaint_type"].where(df["complaint_type"].isin(TYPES), "Other")
mix = ctype_all.value_counts(normalize=True)                     # fixed all-era mix
era_type_p24 = (df.assign(ct=ctype_all).groupby(["era", "ct"], observed=True)["bin"]
                  .apply(lambda s: (s <= 1).mean()).unstack("ct"))
raw_all = df.groupby("era", observed=True)["bin"].apply(lambda s: (s <= 1).mean())
adj_all = (era_type_p24 * mix).sum(axis=1)
adj = pd.DataFrame({"raw P(≤24h)": raw_all.round(3), "mix-adjusted": adj_all.round(3)})
adj.index = [ERA_LABEL[k] for k in adj.index]
adj
```

The gap between the raw and mix-adjusted columns is the composition effect: how much
of each era's apparent speed comes from *what was reported* rather than *how fast it
was handled*. Interpretation in the prose below uses the adjusted view.

## Within the same tract: administration deltas

The citywide picture can hide local reversals. Here we fit the **same hierarchical
Bayesian model that powers the live map** (tract → neighborhood → borough → city,
per complaint type; concentrations by marginal-likelihood MLE) separately to each
era's data, then difference the posterior same-day probabilities tract by tract.
Only tracts with at least 30 requests of that type in *both* eras are compared, so
the deltas reflect local evidence rather than shared priors.

```{python}
#| label: era-fits
#| code-summary: "Fit the hierarchical model per era; compute tract-level deltas"
geo = M.GeoIndex(json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "data", "geo_lookup.json"))))
MIN_TRACT_N = 30
tix = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(TYPES + ["Other"])}

fits, counts = {}, {}
for key in era_keys:
    sub = df[df["era"] == key].copy()
    sub["ctype"] = M.collapse_types(sub["complaint_type"], TYPES)
    fits[key] = M.fit(sub, geo, TYPES + ["Other"], M.Config("era", half_life_days=None),
                      sub["created_date"].max())
    s2 = sub[sub["geoid"].notna()]
    counts[key] = s2.groupby([s2["geoid"], s2["ctype"]], observed=True).size()

def p24_and_var(fm):
    a = fm.a_tract; A = a.sum(-1); Ac = a[..., :2].sum(-1)
    m = Ac / A
    return m, m * (1 - m) / (A + 1)

def tract_deltas(a_key, b_key):
    ma, va = p24_and_var(fits[a_key]); mb, vb = p24_and_var(fits[b_key])
    out = {}
    for t in TYPES:
        ti = tix[t]; recs = []
        for g, gi in geo.tract_ix.items():
            if counts[a_key].get((g, t), 0) < MIN_TRACT_N: continue
            if counts[b_key].get((g, t), 0) < MIN_TRACT_N: continue
            d = ma[gi, ti] - mb[gi, ti]
            se = np.sqrt(va[gi, ti] + vb[gi, ti])
            recs.append((g, d, se))
        if len(recs) >= 25:
            dd = np.array([r[1] for r in recs])
            out[t] = {"recs": recs, "n": len(recs),
                      "med": np.median(dd),
                      "q10": np.percentile(dd, 10), "q90": np.percentile(dd, 90),
                      "up": np.mean([d - 1.645 * s > 0 for _, d, s in recs]),
                      "dn": np.mean([d + 1.645 * s < 0 for _, d, s in recs])}
    return out

D_ad = tract_deltas("adams", "deblasio")
D_ca = tract_deltas("current", "adams")

def delta_table(D):
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "tracts compared": {t.title(): v["n"] for t, v in D.items()},
        "median Δ (pts)": {t.title(): round(100 * v["med"], 1) for t, v in D.items()},
        "10th–90th pct": {t.title(): f'{100*v["q10"]:+.0f} … {100*v["q90"]:+.0f}'
                          for t, v in D.items()},
        "share sig. faster": {t.title(): f'{v["up"]:.0%}' for t, v in D.items()},
        "share sig. slower": {t.title(): f'{v["dn"]:.0%}' for t, v in D.items()},
    }).sort_values("median Δ (pts)", ascending=False)

```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-adams-deblasio
#| tbl-cap: 'Adams vs de Blasio (pre-COVID): change in P(resolved ≤ 24h) within the same tract, by complaint type. "Sig." = the tract''s 90% interval on the change excludes zero.'
#| code-summary: "Delta table: Adams vs de Blasio"
delta_table(D_ad)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-delta-map
#| fig-cap: "Tract-level change in same-day resolution probability, Adams era minus de Blasio (pre-COVID) era, for the mapped complaint type. Green = faster under Adams; purple = slower. Gray tracts lack 30+ requests in both eras."
#| code-summary: "Choropleth of tract deltas"
from matplotlib.collections import PolyCollection
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm

t_map = max(D_ad, key=lambda t: D_ad[t]["n"])       # best-covered type
dm = {g: d for g, d, _ in D_ad[t_map]["recs"]}
gj = json.load(open(os.path.join(ROOT, "web", "data", "tracts.geojson")))

for f in gj["features"]:

        else [p[0] for p in geom["coordinates"]]
    for r in rings:

vals = np.array(vals, dtype=float)
vmax = max(np.nanpercentile(np.abs(vals), 95), .02)

                                 facecolor="#1A2030", edgecolor=C["line"], linewidth=.1))
pc = PolyCollection([p for p, v in zip(polys, vals) if not np.isnan(v)],
                    array=vals[~np.isnan(vals)], cmap="PRGn",
                    norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0, vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax),
                    edgecolor=C["line"], linewidth=.1)
ax.add_collection(pc); ax.autoscale(); ax.set_aspect(1.3); ax.axis("off")
cb = fig.colorbar(pc, ax=ax, shrink=.6, pad=.01)
cb.set_label(f"Δ P(≤24h): {t_map.title()}", color=C["sub"])
cb.ax.yaxis.set_tick_params(color=C["sub"])

             fontsize=12, color=C["text"])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Interpretation

*(This section is written against the rendered numbers above; the inline values
update automatically on re-render.)*

```{python}
#| label: interp-values
#| code-summary: "Values referenced in the prose"
p24 = lambda k, t=None: (era_type_p24.loc[k, t] if t
                         else raw_all.loc[k])
noise_types = [t for t in TYPES if "Noise" in t]
noise_share = {k: df[df["era"] == k]["complaint_type"].isin(noise_types).mean()
               for k in era_keys}
raw_gain = raw_all.loc["adams"] - raw_all.loc["bloomberg"]
adj_gain = adj_all.loc["adams"] - adj_all.loc["bloomberg"]
covid_noise = noise_share.get("covid", float("nan"))
```

Findings that survive the composition and artifact controls:

1. **Most of the all-complaints "improvement" is composition.** Raw same-day
   resolution rose from `{python} f"{raw_all.loc['bloomberg']:.0%}"` (Bloomberg) to
   `{python} f"{raw_all.loc['adams']:.0%}"` (Adams) — but holding the complaint mix
   fixed, the rise is only `{python} f"{adj_all.loc['bloomberg']:.0%}"` →
   `{python} f"{adj_all.loc['adams']:.0%}"`. Roughly
   `{python} f"{1 - adj_gain/raw_gain:.0%}"` of the apparent improvement is the mix
   shifting toward fast-resolving categories (noise complaints grew from
   `{python} f"{noise_share['bloomberg']:.0%}"` of Bloomberg-era volume to
   `{python} f"{noise_share['adams']:.0%}"` under Adams). Any claim that "311 got
   faster under mayor X" that doesn't condition on complaint type is mostly measuring
   New Yorkers' reporting habits.
2. **The clearest operational pattern is agency-shaped, not administration-shaped.**
   Housing types (all handled by HPD) improved *monotonically across every era*:
   same-day resolution of Heat/Hot Water went
   `{python} f"{p24('bloomberg','HEAT/HOT WATER'):.0%}"` →
   `{python} f"{p24('deblasio','HEAT/HOT WATER'):.0%}"` →
   `{python} f"{p24('adams','HEAT/HOT WATER'):.0%}"` from Bloomberg to de Blasio to
   Adams, with Plumbing, Electric, and Paint/Plaster showing the same staircase from
   near-zero. Meanwhile infrastructure types slipped across the same span — Water
   System `{python} f"{p24('bloomberg','Water System'):.0%}"` →
   `{python} f"{p24('adams','Water System'):.0%}"`, Traffic Signals
   `{python} f"{p24('bloomberg','Traffic Signal Condition'):.0%}"` →
   `{python} f"{p24('adams','Traffic Signal Condition'):.0%}"` — and police-handled
   types (parking, noise) have been saturated near 99% for sixteen years. Secular
   agency trajectories dominate administration boundaries.
3. **Within types, administrations were not uniform across neighborhoods** — see
   @tbl-adams-deblasio: the 10th–90th percentile spread of tract-level changes is
   wide even where the median change is small, and the tract map shows spatial
   clustering rather than uniform shifts.
4. **COVID was a composition shock more than a slowdown.** The raw all-complaints
   series *rose* during 2020–21, because lockdown-era noise complaints surged to
   `{python} f"{covid_noise:.0%}"` of all volume; per-type effects ran in both
   directions (heat improved, derelict-vehicle and traffic-signal work slowed). This
   is exactly why the COVID window is quarantined and why the mix-adjusted row is
   the one to read.
5. **The Mamdani administration's record is provisional** (@tbl-current-adams).
   Zohran Mamdani took office in January 2026, succeeding Eric Adams, so this era covers
   only the months of 2026 that have matured, is missing the autumn and early-winter
   months that every other era includes, and is best treated as a baseline for future
   updates rather than a verdict.

## Why the live map still trains on recent data only

The dashboard deliberately ignores this history when estimating *current* odds. Its
evaluation selected a 90-day exponential decay: under that weighting a two-year-old
request carries weight `{python} f"{2**(-730/90):.4f}"` — effectively zero — and the
prior comparison showed shorter memory beats longer memory for near-term prediction
(`docs/evaluation_results.md`). History answers "what changed"; the last two years
answer "what should I expect if I call today." Those are different questions, and
this document exists so the map doesn't have to answer both.

## Caveats, stated plainly

- **Recorded ≠ experienced.** Closure timestamps are administrative events. Era
  differences partly reflect record-keeping practice; batch-closure and never-closed
  rates are quantified in the era context table.
- **Bloomberg = final term only.** The public dataset begins 2010; nothing here
  speaks to 2002–2009.
- **Geocoding improves over time** (86% of 2010 requests are tract-mappable vs ~98%
  today), so early-era tract comparisons rest on a slightly thinner, possibly
  non-random subset of requests.
- **Taxonomy drift is handled conservatively**: only unambiguous renames are merged,
  and analysis is restricted to types present in every era. Types born after 2014
  (e.g., outdoor dining complaints) are simply out of scope for the long arc.
- **Administrations are periods, not causes.** Nothing here identifies *why* a
  probability moved — budgets, laws, weather, and reporting behavior all changed
  concurrently. This is a descriptive account of associations within fixed geography.

## Technical addendum: modeling decisions, sensitivity, and robustness {#sec-addendum}

This appendix records the decisions behind the machinery this analysis reuses, and the
checks run along the way. Numbers quoted from prior evaluations are the documented
outputs of the pipeline's own harnesses (`docs/evaluation_results.md`,
`docs/statistical_review.md`); everything specific to *this* document is computed in
the chunks above.

### Model class

The estimator throughout is a hierarchical Dirichlet–Multinomial over the nine ordered
duration bins, with partial pooling tract → NTA → borough → citywide, fit as a
top-down conjugate cascade (each node's Dirichlet prior is κ pseudo-counts shaped like
its parent's posterior mean). Alternatives considered and rejected: continuous-time
survival models (non-conjugate inference at 40M rows for a deliverable that is the
binned distribution anyway); continuation-ratio Beta–Binomial stacks (equally
conjugate but no actual adjacent-bin smoothing without breaking conjugacy — bin order
is instead respected at evaluation time via the ranked probability score); and full
hierarchical Bayes with sampled concentrations (too slow for a weekly refresh of every
cell). The plug-in shortcut was then checked against a fully Bayesian Stan fit for one
borough and three complaint types: tract means differ by 0.7–1.1 points on average
(`docs/stan_validation.md`). Pooling runs within complaint type across geography, not
across types within a tract, because resolution speed is owned by the responsible agency,
not the neighborhood.

### Configuration contest (live map)

Nine configurations were compared on a temporal holdout (train 2024-08 → 2025-08,
test the following 12 months; all hyperparameters fit on train only), scored by mean RPS
(primary), log-loss, calibration error, and interval calibration, with paired
block-bootstrap SEs over tract×type cells (`docs/evaluation_results.md`):

| configuration | RPS | vs. best |
|---|---|---|
| No pooling (uniform / Jeffreys) | 0.10685 / 0.10548 | +0.00395 / +0.00258 |
| Hierarchy, fixed κ=15 | 0.10365 | +0.00075 |
| Hierarchy, EB κ (per type / per type-level) | 0.10316 / 0.10318 | +0.00026 / +0.00028 |
| **+ 90-day decay (shipped)** | **0.10302** | +0.00012 |
| + 180-day / 365-day decay | 0.10290 / 0.10297 | best / +0.00007 |

The no-pooling baselines' failure mode is exact and diagnostic: on tract×type cells
unseen in training they predict the bare prior — uniform over nine bins, log-loss
log(9) = 2.197 — while the hierarchy falls back to the neighborhood estimate (1.73–1.88).

This single split trains once and predicts up to a year ahead, which favors long memory
and is not how the map is used; the weekly-refit setting is tested by a rolling-origin
evaluation that refits at each month start and scores only that month
(`docs/rolling_evaluation.md`). There, half-lives of 45 to 180 days are statistically
tied with the shipped 90 days (differences of 0.00000 to +0.00004 RPS), 365 days is worse
by 0.00014 ± 0.00005, and no decay by 0.00040 ± 0.00008, so 90 days stays.

### Defects found by audit, all fixed

Adversarial computational audits (independent re-implementation of the cascade;
verification of every exported cell against the raw files) found:

1. **Concentration estimation under-converged.** Minka's fixed-point iteration stalled
   far short of the marginal-likelihood optimum on these flat surfaces (tract-level
   Heat/Hot Water: κ ≈ 230 vs true optimum ≈ 800, a 78-nat likelihood gap;
   Illegal Parking: 87 vs ≈ 400, 288 nats). The estimator now maximizes the exact
   Dirichlet–Multinomial marginal likelihood by bounded scalar optimization.
   Predictions moved negligibly (the flat surface is why the defect was silent), but
   pooling strengths are now genuine MLEs — including the era fits above.
2. **Raw posterior intervals badly under-covered.** In the original audit, coverage of
   nominal 90% intervals on dense cells was 0.25–0.51 — including on an even/odd
   day-of-year split where drift is impossible by construction, refuting an initial
   "temporal drift" explanation. The live map's intervals now add a per-type,
   per-threshold regime variance estimated from rolling 60-day temporal holdouts; on the
   current data, coverage is 0.908 in dense cells and about 0.90 in sparse ones
   (squared standardized residual 1.14). A multiplicative (design-effect) correction was
   tested and rejected — it absurdly inflates sparse-cell intervals. Why the even/odd-day
   shortfall occurred (correlated outcomes within cells is the working hypothesis) has
   not been tested directly.
3. **Requests without a tract were counted in one tract.** Under pandas 2, converting the
   tract column with `astype(str)` turned missing values into the text "nan", so about
   1.6% of requests were counted in Rikers Island (tract 36005000100); pandas 3 keeps them
   missing, so the result depended on the installed version. Fixed, verified across
   versions, and guarded by export checks (`docs/statistical_review.md` §7). The era fits
   in this report were not affected: they load the data with their own null handling.
4. **Interval theory ignored the uncertainty of the borrowed neighborhood mean.** A
   simulation with known truth showed 43–81% coverage for nominal 90% intervals even when
   the data follow the model exactly; the interval variance now includes that term
   (`docs/simulation_check.md`). On real data the regime variance dominates, so users see
   almost no change.

### Sensitivity and robustness checks run

- **Decay half-life**: rolling-origin comparison over 11 monthly refits (see above);
  45–180 days are tied, 365 days and no decay are worse.
- **Seasonal blending**: a same-season-last-year kernel (conjugate, weight
  β·2^(−|age−1yr|/bw)) was re-tested with two years of history under the same rolling
  protocol. The best variant improves RPS by 0.00013 ± 0.00004 and log-loss by
  0.00176 ± 0.00038 but wins in only 5 of the 11 months, so it is not adopted
  (`pipeline/eval_rolling.py`).
- **Pooling strength per threshold**: fitting a separate strength for each cumulative
  threshold improves held-out log-loss slightly at all eight thresholds, but is mixed by
  type and marginal for the all-complaints view; not adopted (`docs/cutwise_evaluation.md`).
  This bears on this report: the tract-level era comparisons use the nine-bin pooling, so
  for types where that over-pools the 24-hour rate, tract-level changes between eras are
  understated (conservative), not overstated.
- **Censoring**: the 31-day maturity cutoff is keyed to the top bin boundary, making
  the "still open ⇒ month+" assignment deductively exact rather than imputed;
  verified against pull dates. Composition of the month+ bin was audited on the original
  window: 8.8% of matured requests land there, 28.5% of those never close; for
  Heat/Hot Water >99% of month+ cases are administrative non-closures — reported as-is
  with a high-open-share flag.
- **Cleaning funnel** (current live window): 7.52M → 7.08M rows; about 286k
  double-submissions collapsed, 131k exact-zero durations dropped, 114k batch closures
  flagged and *kept* (dropping them would optimistically bias slow agencies). A full
  evaluation re-run excluding batch-flagged records remains open; for this document their
  per-era rates are disclosed in the era context table instead.
- **Independent audit** (`pipeline/audit.py`): raw rows reconcile with the funnel; every
  tract × type count matches an independent tally; binning is correct at the bin
  boundaries; a separate re-implementation of the cascade reproduces all 51,150 cells; and
  one month recomputed from the raw files agrees with the pipeline to 0.1 point.
- **RPS implementation** verified against hand computation; bootstrap resamples
  cells, not requests (within-cell correlation would otherwise understate SEs).

### Choices specific to this historical analysis

- **Era fits use no decay**: the estimand is each era's average recorded behavior,
  not a nowcast. Concentrations are re-estimated per era, so pooling strength adapts
  to each era's data density.
- **Stable-type restriction** (≥15k requests in every era) plus conservative 1:1
  rename normalization; types that split or merged across the 2014 taxonomy overhaul
  are excluded rather than guessed at.
- **Tract deltas require n ≥ 30 in both eras** so differences reflect local evidence
  rather than two shared priors agreeing with each other; interval on the delta is
  the normal combination of the two independent Beta variances. This intentionally
  reports *sampling* uncertainty for a fixed-era estimand — the regime-variance
  component the live map adds is a forecasting correction and would be wrong here.
- **Composition adjustment** fixes the complaint mix at the pooled all-era
  distribution; the raw-vs-adjusted gap isolates how much of each era's apparent
  speed is reporting mix.
- **COVID quarantine** (2020-03 – 2021-12) keeps an extraordinary operating regime
  out of both adjacent administrations' records.
- **Known residual risks**: geocoding coverage drift (86% → 98% tract-mappable);
  recorded-vs-experienced resolution; single-observation seasonality in the
  partial-year Mamdani era (2026), which lacks autumn and early winter.

### Reproduction

```
python3 pipeline/fetch_311.py            # rolling two-year window
python3 pipeline/fetch_311_history.py    # 2010-2024 archive (~38M rows)
python3 pipeline/prepare.py && python3 pipeline/prepare_hist.py --all
quarto render docs/historical_analysis.qmd
```

Full detail: `docs/model_spec.md` (specification), `docs/evaluation_results.md` and
`docs/rolling_evaluation.md` (evaluation), `docs/statistical_review.md` (audits),
`docs/METHODS.md` (public methods).
